source_en: Emergency contraception is a way to prevent pregnancy after sex has already happened, for example after sex without a condom or when a condom broke. The World Health Organization describes four options: emergency pills containing levonorgestrel, pills containing ulipristal acetate, a special dose of ordinary combined pills, and the copper IUD, which a health worker fits inside the womb. Taken within 5 days, emergency pills can prevent most pregnancies, and the sooner they are used the better they work. In Ethiopia, emergency pills and the copper IUD are the available options. Emergency contraception is safe for any woman or girl of reproductive age, with no age limit, so it is completely fine to ask a pharmacy or clinic for it.
target_am: ድንገተኛ የእርግዝና መከላከያ ማለት የግብረ ሥጋ ግንኙነት ከተፈጸመ በኋላ እርግዝናን ለመከላከል የሚያገለግል ዘዴ ነው። ለምሳሌ Condom ሳይጠቀሙ ግንኙነት ሲፈጸም ወይም Condom ሲቀደድ ይጠቅማል። የዓለም ጤና ድርጅት አራት አማራጮችን ይገልጻል፦ levonorgestrel የያዙ ክኒኖች፣ ulipristal acetate የያዙ ክኒኖች፣ የተቀናጁ የወሊድ መከላከያ ክኒኖች በልዩ መጠን፣ እና በጤና ባለሙያ በማህፀን ውስጥ የሚገባ የመዳብ IUD። በ5 ቀናት ውስጥ ከተወሰዱ ድንገተኛ ክኒኖች አብዛኞቹን እርግዝናዎች መከላከል ይችላሉ፤ ቶሎ በተወሰዱ ቁጥር ውጤታማነታቸው ይጨምራል። በኢትዮጵያ የሚገኙት አማራጮች ድንገተኛ ክኒኖች እና የመዳብ IUD ናቸው። ድንገተኛ መከላከያ በመውለድ ዕድሜ ላሉ ሴቶች ሁሉ ደህንነቱ የተጠበቀ ነው፤ የዕድሜ ገደብ የለውም። ስለዚህ ከመድኃኒት ቤት ወይም ከጤና ተቋም መጠየቅ ምንም የሚያሳፍር ነገር አይደለም።

source_en: Act quickly, because emergency contraception works best soon after sex. The levonorgestrel pill, often sold as Levonelle or Postpill, should be taken within 3 days, meaning 72 hours, after sex. The ulipristal acetate pill, such as ellaOne, can work up to 5 days, meaning 120 hours, after sex. A copper IUD can be fitted by a health worker within 5 days and is the most effective option of all. Whichever method you choose, the sooner you use it, the more effective it usually is, so do not wait for the next morning if you can go today. Pharmacies and health centres can help the same day, and asking for it is a responsible choice, nothing to be ashamed of.
target_am: በፍጥነት እርምጃ ይውሰዱ፤ ድንገተኛ መከላከያ ከግንኙነት በኋላ ቶሎ ሲወሰድ በተሻለ ይሠራል። levonorgestrel ክኒን (ብዙ ጊዜ Postpill ተብሎ የሚሸጠው) ከግንኙነት በኋላ በ3 ቀናት ማለትም በ72 ሰዓታት ውስጥ መወሰድ አለበት። ulipristal acetate ክኒን እስከ 5 ቀናት ማለትም እስከ 120 ሰዓታት ድረስ ሊሠራ ይችላል። የመዳብ IUD በጤና ባለሙያ በ5 ቀናት ውስጥ ሊገባ ይችላል፤ ከሁሉም አማራጮች በላይ ውጤታማው እሱ ነው። የትኛውንም ዘዴ ቢመርጡ ቶሎ ሲጠቀሙ ውጤታማነቱ ይጨምራል፤ ዛሬ መሄድ ከቻሉ ነገ አይጠብቁ። መድኃኒት ቤቶች እና ጤና ጣቢያዎች በዚያው ቀን ሊረዱ ይችላሉ፤ ይህን መጠየቅ ኃላፊነት የተሞላበት ውሳኔ እንጂ የሚያሳፍር አይደለም።

source_en: No. Emergency contraception does not cause abortion. The World Health Organization is clear that emergency contraception cannot interrupt an established pregnancy and cannot harm a developing embryo. It works by preventing a pregnancy from starting after sex; once a pregnancy has begun, emergency pills have no effect on it. This is why health workers describe it as contraception, not abortion. It is also safe: WHO states there are no absolute medical contraindications to its use, and Ethiopia's national guideline says the same, that no known medical condition prevents someone from using emergency pills. Side effects, when they happen, are mild things like nausea or slight irregular bleeding that pass on their own. Using emergency contraception is a safe, legitimate way to prevent an unwanted pregnancy.
target_am: አይደለም። ድንገተኛ የእርግዝና መከላከያ ውርጃ አያስከትልም። የዓለም ጤና ድርጅት በግልጽ እንደሚናገረው፣ ድንገተኛ መከላከያ የተጀመረን እርግዝና ማቋረጥ አይችልም፤ በማደግ ላይ ያለ ጽንስንም አይጎዳም። የሚሠራው ከግንኙነት በኋላ እርግዝና ከመጀመሩ በፊት በመከላከል ነው፤ እርግዝና ከተጀመረ በኋላ ድንገተኛ ክኒኖች በእሱ ላይ ምንም ውጤት የላቸውም። ለዚህ ነው የጤና ባለሙያዎች መከላከያ እንጂ ውርጃ አይደለም የሚሉት። ደህንነቱም የተጠበቀ ነው፤ የዓለም ጤና ድርጅት ፍጹም የሆነ የህክምና ክልከላ እንደሌለው ይገልጻል፤ የኢትዮጵያ ብሔራዊ መመሪያም ድንገተኛ ክኒን መውሰድን የሚከለክል የታወቀ የጤና ችግር እንደሌለ ያረጋግጣል። የጎንዮሽ ጉዳቶች ሲከሰቱ እንደ ማቅለሽለሽ ወይም ቀላል መደበኛ ያልሆነ መድማት ያሉ ቀላል ችግሮች ናቸው፤ በራሳቸው ያልፋሉ።

source_en: No. Emergency contraception does not cause infertility. The World Health Organization states plainly that the drugs used for emergency contraception do not harm future fertility, and that there is no delay in the return to fertility after taking them. This means a woman can become pregnant again in the very next cycle if she has unprotected sex, so ongoing contraception still matters. Side effects of emergency pills are mild and temporary, things like nausea, tiredness, or slight irregular bleeding, and they resolve on their own. Because emergency contraception is so safe, WHO says any woman or girl of reproductive age can use it, with no absolute medical restrictions. Worry about future children should never stop someone from preventing a pregnancy they do not want today.
target_am: አይደለም። ድንገተኛ የእርግዝና መከላከያ መካንነት አያስከትልም። የዓለም ጤና ድርጅት በግልጽ እንደሚናገረው፣ ለድንገተኛ መከላከያ የሚያገለግሉ መድኃኒቶች የወደፊት የመውለድ ችሎታን አይጎዱም፤ የመውለድ ችሎታ መመለስም አይዘገይም። ይህ ማለት ጥንቃቄ ከሌለ በሚቀጥለው ወር እንኳን ማርገዝ ይቻላል፤ ስለዚህ ቀጣይ መከላከያ አሁንም ያስፈልጋል። የድንገተኛ ክኒኖች የጎንዮሽ ጉዳቶች እንደ ማቅለሽለሽ፣ ድካም ወይም ቀላል መደበኛ ያልሆነ መድማት ያሉ ቀላልና ጊዜያዊ ናቸው፤ በራሳቸው ይጠፋሉ። ድንገተኛ መከላከያ በጣም ደህንነቱ የተጠበቀ ስለሆነ በመውለድ ዕድሜ ያለች ማንኛዋም ሴት ልትጠቀመው ትችላለች። ስለወደፊት ልጆች መጨነቅ ዛሬ የማይፈለግ እርግዝናን ከመከላከል ሊያግድ አይገባም።

source_en: Yes, emergency contraception can be used more than once. The World Health Organization states that repeated use of emergency contraceptive pills poses no known health risks, so nobody should be refused it because they have used it before. WHO does note that frequent, repeated use may be harmful for women with certain specific medical conditions, which is one reason a chat with a health worker is useful for someone using it often. It is also worth knowing that the copper IUD is the most effective form of emergency contraception, and a regular method like the implant, pill, or condoms gives better ongoing protection than relying on emergency pills each time. Using emergency contraception again is far safer than risking an unwanted pregnancy.

source_en: A condom prevents pregnancy by acting as a physical barrier during sex, so semen and sperm stay inside the condom instead of entering the vagina. Laboratory studies show latex condoms are an effective barrier even to the smallest infection-causing organisms, which is why they also protect against HIV and other STIs; the NHS calls using a condom every time the best way to protect both partners. Used perfectly every time, condoms are up to 98% effective at preventing pregnancy. With typical real-life use they are about 82% effective, meaning around 1 in 5 women relying on condoms for a year may become pregnant, usually because of incorrect or inconsistent use. Check the expiry date, use a new condom each time, and only use water-based or silicone-based lubricant with latex condoms.

source_en: If a condom breaks or slips off, do not panic, but act quickly. There are two things to think about: pregnancy and infection. For pregnancy, emergency contraception may be needed, and it must be used within 3 to 5 days of sex depending on the type, with the sooner the better. A pharmacist, health centre, or sexual health clinic can provide it, often the same day. For infection, a condom failure counts as unprotected sex, so an STI test is worth considering, and if there is any chance of HIV exposure, ask a health provider promptly about post-exposure prophylaxis, medicine that can prevent HIV after exposure. Condom breakage happens to many people; getting help quickly is the responsible next step, not something to be embarrassed about.

source_en: No, the pill does not cause infertility. The NHS states that when you stop taking the combined pill, your fertility usually returns to previous levels after about a month. Ethiopia's national family planning guideline agrees, noting that most modern contraceptive methods do not cause a significant delay in the return to fertility. The pill works by stopping the ovaries from releasing an egg each month, and this effect only lasts while you keep taking it. Taken correctly all the time, it is over 99% effective; with typical use, about 9 in 100 women become pregnant in a year, usually because of missed pills. So the pill protects you now and does not take away your chance of having children later.

source_en: Yes, changes in bleeding are very common with the implant, and for most people they are not a sign that anything is wrong. The implant releases the hormone progestogen, which stops the ovaries releasing an egg each month, and this hormone also changes bleeding patterns. The NHS explains that periods may become lighter, less regular with spotting between periods, heavier or more painful, longer lasting, or may stop completely, and the pattern can be unpredictable from month to month. The NHS says these changes are not usually anything to worry about. The implant itself remains over 99% effective whatever the bleeding pattern. If the bleeding becomes a problem for you, a doctor or sexual health clinic can help, and there are often options to manage it.

source_en: No, the implant does not cause infertility. The NHS states that once the implant is removed, your chance of getting pregnant returns to what it was before the implant was fitted, straight away. There is no waiting period for fertility to come back, which is why anyone removing an implant who does not want a pregnancy needs another method immediately. source_en: Most pregnancy tests can be done from the first day of a missed period. If you are not sure when your period is due, the NHS advises doing the test at least 21 days after you last had unprotected sex. Tests work by detecting a hormone called human chorionic gonadotrophin, or hCG, in urine. The body starts producing hCG around 6 days after fertilisation, but levels take time to rise high enough for a test to detect, which is why testing too early can miss a real pregnancy. Some very sensitive tests can work slightly before a missed period. A positive result is almost certainly correct, so it can be trusted. A negative result is less reliable, especially if the test was done early.

source_en: A pregnancy test can show negative even when a period is late for two main reasons. First, the test may have been done too early, before the pregnancy hormone hCG rose high enough to detect, or the instructions may not have been followed properly. The NHS notes that a negative result is less reliable than a positive one. If you still think you might be pregnant, wait a few days and test again. Second, the period may be late for a reason other than pregnancy: stress, sudden weight change, too much exercise, hormonal contraception, and some health conditions can all delay or stop periods. If a second test is negative and your period has still not arrived, see a doctor to find out what is going on.

source_en: Pregnancy from sex during a period is unlikely, but it cannot be ruled out, so bleeding is not a form of contraception. Here is why. Pregnancy happens around ovulation, which in most women occurs around 10 to 16 days before the next period, and that timing shifts from cycle to cycle. Sperm can survive in the fallopian tubes for up to 7 days after sex. So if someone has a short cycle or ovulates early, sperm from sex during or just after a period can still be alive when an egg is released. The NHS confirms it is possible, although not very likely, to get pregnant soon after a period finishes. Anyone not ready for pregnancy should use contraception at every act of sex, whatever the day of the cycle.

source_en: Withdrawal, or pulling out, is one of the least reliable ways to prevent pregnancy. On the CDC's effectiveness chart, 22 out of every 100 women whose partners use withdrawal become pregnant within the first year of typical use. Compare that with about 18 for condoms, 9 for the pill, and fewer than 1 for the implant. Withdrawal means completely removing the penis from the vagina and away from the outside genitals before ejaculation, and in real life the timing often fails. It also gives no protection at all against STIs, including HIV. Pregnancy can even happen when sperm merely contacts the vagina. If avoiding pregnancy matters to you, a condom or another modern method is a far safer choice, and clinics can help you pick one.

source_en: A late period has many possible causes, and pregnancy is only one of them. The NHS lists pregnancy, stress, sudden weight loss, being overweight, and doing too much exercise as common reasons. Hormonal contraception such as the pill, the injection, or a hormonal IUS can also change or stop periods, and so can breastfeeding. Hormonal conditions matter too: polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and the start of menopause, usually between ages 45 and 55, can both stop periods. If pregnancy is possible, do a test from the first day of the missed period. See a doctor if you have missed three periods in a row, if periods have become irregular, or if a missed period comes with symptoms like weight change, tiredness, or new facial hair growth.

source_en: Pregnancy is possible during a window of days around ovulation, when an egg is released from the ovary. The NHS explains that in most women ovulation happens around 10 to 16 days before the next period, and someone with a regular 28-day cycle is likely to be fertile around day 14. The fertile window is wider than the day of ovulation itself, because sperm can survive in the fallopian tubes for up to 7 days after sex, so sex in the days before ovulation can still lead to pregnancy. Timing shifts between cycles, and with early ovulation or a short cycle, pregnancy is possible soon after a period finishes. Because the fertile days are hard to predict exactly, counting days alone is a risky way to avoid pregnancy.

source_en: Yes. Most sexually transmitted infections cause no symptoms at all, so a person can have an STI, feel completely well, and still pass it to a partner. The World Health Organization reports that more than 1 million curable STIs are acquired every day worldwide among people aged 15 to 49, and the majority of these infections are asymptomatic. Even when symptoms do appear, they can be vague and easy to mistake for something else. This is why feeling fine is not proof of being infection free, and why testing matters after unprotected sex or a new partner. Signs like unusual discharge from the vagina or penis, or sores and ulcers around the genitals, should always prompt a visit to a health facility, but silence from the body is not an all-clear.

source_en: STI risk can be brought down a great deal with a few practical steps. The World Health Organization states that when used correctly and consistently, condoms offer one of the most effective methods of protection against STIs, and the NHS calls using a condom every time you have sex the best way to protect yourself and your partner from HIV and other STIs. Ethiopia's national guideline strongly recommends dual protection, meaning condoms used to prevent both pregnancy and infection, for anyone at risk of STIs and HIV. Safe and highly effective vaccines exist for two viral STIs, hepatitis B and HPV. Finally, if one partner is diagnosed, treating sexual partners is an important part of care, so encourage a partner to get tested and treated too.

source_en: HIV is not spread through everyday contact. The World Health Organization states that people cannot become infected with HIV through ordinary day-to-day contact such as kissing, hugging, shaking hands, or sharing personal objects, food, or water. So sharing a meal, a cup, a bathroom, a classroom, or a home with someone living with HIV carries no risk, and neither does a handshake or a hug. HIV is only transmitted through the exchange of certain body fluids from a person living with HIV, namely blood, breast milk, semen, and vaginal secretions, and from mother to child during pregnancy and delivery. Knowing this protects people living with HIV from unfair fear and stigma, and helps everyone focus on the real routes of transmission and the real means of prevention, like condoms and treatment.

source_en: The window period is the time between HIV exposure and when a test can detect HIV in the body. During this time a test can be negative even though the person has HIV and can pass it on. The World Health Organization notes that most people develop antibodies to HIV within 28 days of infection, so antibody tests may miss a very recent infection, and anyone testing negative after a recent exposure should retest after 28 days. The CDC gives windows by test type: nucleic acid tests detect HIV 10 to 33 days after exposure, laboratory antigen/antibody tests 18 to 45 days, rapid antigen/antibody tests 18 to 90 days, and antibody self-tests 23 to 90 days. If a test after possible exposure is negative, test again once the window for that test has passed.
